content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines in 2015 addressing mental health in the workplace. Annex 4 of these guidelines provides a detailed review of the evidence and supporting data used to answer key questions. The evidence review process involved identifying systematic reviews from databases such as the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and Global Index Medicus. These reviews were selected based on their relevance to specific Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcomes (PICO) questions. If no suitable reviews were available within the past five years, the search timeframe was extended to a maximum of ten years. The identified reviews were evaluated using the AMSTAR II tool, which assesses the methodological quality of systematic reviews. Key criteria included the presence of study characteristics, risk-of-bias assessments, and meta-analysis results. The most recent and highest-quality reviews, as determined by AMSTAR II ratings, were prioritized. Randomized designs were given preference, but controlled observational designs were also considered due to their relevance in occupational settings. For two key questions (4 and 5), existing reviews were updated to include additional studies. For question 13, where no systematic review existed, a new systematic review of primary studies was conducted. In total, 36 systematic reviews, nine additional primary studies, and one network meta-analysis were included. Supplementary evidence was also gathered to address gaps in the literature, particularly in light of global changes in work modes due to the COVID-19 pandemic. This included a mixed-methods survey to capture the values and preferences of key stakeholders (e.g., workers, employers, mental health service providers, and union representatives) and a semi-structured interview with experts to explore the needs of the informal sector. A qualitative research review was commissioned to identify barriers and facilitators to implementing workplace mental health interventions. The GRADE-CerQual tool was used to assess the confidence in qualitative evidence findings, while the GRADE system was applied to evaluate the certainty of quantitative evidence. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) assessed the certainty of evidence to determine how confidently recommendations could be made. Evidence profiles summarizing relative and absolute effect estimates, along with certainty assessments, were presented to the GDG for discussion. Recommendations were formulated using a structured Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework, which considered factors such as the priority of the problem, evidence certainty, balance of effects, values, resource requirements, cost-effectiveness, feasibility, equity, human rights, and sociocultural acceptability. Recommendations were classified as either strong or conditional, depending on the confidence in the balance of desirable versus undesirable effects. The GDG met virtually in June 2021 to discuss and agree on the recommendations. Meetings were held in duplicate sessions to accommodate time zone differences. Recommendations were finalized through consensus, defined as a two-thirds majority vote. If major disagreements arose, the GDG agreed to reconvene, though this was not necessary. The Responsible Technical Officer drafted the guidelines, which were reviewed by the GDG and an External Review Group (ERG). Peer review comments were addressed by the WHO Steering Group, ensuring clarity and consistency with the original recommendations. The guidelines underwent WHO’s internal approval and quality assurance process to meet international standards. They were reviewed and approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee (GRC) before being prepared for publication and dissemination.
